title: Neighborhood Housing Trends
text:
Project


An interactive R Shiny app for exploring home values and recent price changes across neighborhoods in a given city. Follow this link to try the app yourself: Neighborhood Housing Trends





Screenshot of Neighborhood Housing Trends app






Interactive mapping application



R, Shiny, Leaflet, sf, dplyr



Housing trends by neighborhood, presented in an interactive interface




This project grew out of an interest in making housing data easier to explore at a local level. Housing discussions often jump quickly to state or national averages, but those summaries can hide the fact that nearby places may be moving in very different ways. I wanted to build something more grounded: a tool that lets a user explore how prices and growth vary across neighborhoods in a given city.
The result is an interactive application built in R with Shiny. It combines housing data with geographic boundaries and presents the results through a map-based interface, so the user can see neighborhood level housing trends.

The aim was not just to display data, but to make neighborhood variation easier to notice and easier to interpret.




In practical terms, this is most useful for people trying to understand a city at a neighborhood level. Someone considering a move can quickly compare affordability and recent price trends across areas, while someone working in housing or development can use it as a fast way to scan for local differences worth investigating further.
The aim is not to answer every question, but to make the first pass through the data easier and more informative.




An interactive map interface for exploring housing trends at a neighborhood level
Views centered on home values and recent change over time
A structure that combines geographic boundaries with housing data in a way that supports quick and easy comparison

I was especially interested in building a project that moved beyond a static chart. The map interface makes it possible to scan for broad patterns first and then narrow in on places that look unusual or worth investigating further.



The repository uses Zillow Home Value Index data and Census boundary data, and the codebase is written entirely in R. The repository includes an app.R file for the Shiny application along with supporting data and scripts, and the current README describes the project as an analysis of neighborhood housing trends. :contentReferenceoaicite:0
From a tooling perspective, this project sits in a space I like a great deal: lightweight analytical tools that are technically serious but still readable. The emphasis was on using R not just for analysis, but also for presentation.



This project reinforced a lesson that comes up often in quantitative work: once the core analysis is in place, the next challenge is usually one of structure. What should be compared? What deserves visual emphasis? What makes a user trust what they are seeing?
It also reminded me that interactive projects benefit from restraint. A useful map does not need ten controls or a complicated story. It needs a few meaningful comparisons, a clear visual hierarchy, and enough context for the user to stay oriented.

title: Shuler Hopkins
text:
Quantitative analysis, tutoring, and project support — done carefully, and explained clearly.


I work with students, researchers, and small organizations on statistical and analytical problems that need more than a quick answer. My background is in mathematics, data science, and teaching, and I tend to approach projects with equal attention to correctness, clarity, and structure.


Services Projects Contact

shuler.hopkins7@gmail.com






Data cleaning, exploratory analysis, regression, hypothesis testing, and interpretation for projects that need clear reasoning and useful results.



One-on-one support in statistics, calculus, and data analysis, with an emphasis on understanding rather than memorization.



Short-term help with research workflows, technical writing, reports, and lightweight analytical tools built in R.





I like work that is technically sound, visually clean, and honest about uncertainty. In practice, that usually means starting with the real question, keeping the methods proportionate to the problem, and communicating results in a way that another person can actually use.



I have a Ph.D. in Mathematics and experience teaching mathematics, statistics, data science, and computer science. Much of my work has involved organizing difficult material, building structure around it, and making it more understandable to the people who need it.



Right now, I am especially interested in applied statistics, analytical communication, education, and small tools that make quantitative work more approachable.

Built with Quarto and R. Keeping things simple.

title: Services
text:
I help with statistical analysis, quantitative tutoring, and project-based analytical work, especially when the problem is real but the path forward is not yet clear.






Help with data cleaning, exploratory analysis, regression, hypothesis testing, interpretation, and presenting results clearly.
This is a good fit for research projects, independent studies, theses, or applied questions where the data exists but the path forward is unclear.



One-on-one support in statistics, calculus, data analysis, and related quantitative coursework.
I am especially well suited for students who want more than procedural help and need someone who can explain the logic behind the methods.



Short-term help with technical reports, research workflows, analytical tools, and quantitative writeups.
This is often most useful when a project needs structure, revision, or a second pair of eyes from someone comfortable with both details and communication.





My work is usually most useful for a few kinds of people:

students working through statistics, calculus, or data analysis
researchers with data they need help cleaning, analyzing, or explaining
people with a technical or analytical project that needs structure
small organizations that need clear, careful quantitative help without a large consulting engagement

In general, I am a good fit for projects where the main need is not just computation, but judgment: choosing a reasonable method, organizing the work clearly, and explaining the result in plain language.



I prefer to begin with the actual problem rather than a predetermined method. Sometimes that leads to a model or a formal test; sometimes it leads to a simpler answer, which is often better.
My bias is toward work that is: - technically sound - clearly written - proportionate to the question - honest about uncertainty
I am generally less interested in adding complexity for its own sake than in making the work accurate, readable, and useful.



Depending on the project, that might include:

helping clean and organize a dataset
identifying an appropriate statistical approach
checking and improving a quantitative writeup
building simple visualizations or summaries in R
walking through a difficult topic one-on-one
helping shape a project that has become too broad or disorganized




The work I do is usually best when the question is real and the person asking it is engaged. I am probably not the right fit for situations where someone wants a rushed answer with no interest in understanding the reasoning. I am a much better fit for people who want careful work, clear explanation, and a finished result that makes sense.



If you have a project or question, feel free to reach out.
shuler.hopkins7@gmail.com
